# Colors, Named

Marguerite names paint colors for a living, which people find either delightful or ridiculous, and she has stopped trying to predict which.

The job is this: a chemist in Ohio mixes a new shade, a spectrophotometer turns it into numbers, and the numbers arrive in her inbox with a small square of the color itself, which never looks the same on two screens. She stares at the square and gives it a name. The company pays her by the batch. Forty colors, forty names, due Friday.

Most of the names are not hers. They belong to the catalog, to the voice the catalog has had since before she arrived: *Harbor Mist. Morning Oat. Quiet Birch.* Nouns that sound like a house you could afford if you made different choices. Her first year, she tried to name a gray *Parking Garage at Dusk*, and her editor, a kind man named Philip, wrote back: *Accurate. Devastating. No.*

So she learned the voice. She got good at it. She can produce *Soft Heron* in her sleep.

---

The year her marriage ended, something went wrong with the job, or possibly right.

It started with a brown. Warm, a little red underneath, the color of wet clay or a strong tea left too long. She looked at the square and thought, without meaning to, of the coffee table David had refinished the first summer they lived together. He'd done it in the driveway because the apartment had no garage. He'd sanded it for three weekends, shirtless, cursing, and when he finally stained it, the stain went on exactly this color. She'd brought him a beer and he'd said, *Well, it's ours now,* as if labor were the thing that made furniture belong to you.

She typed *Driveway Table*. Then she deleted it and typed *Summer Walnut*, because that was the voice.

But the next square was a pale green, and it was the green of the hospital curtain the night his father died, the curtain they had both stared at rather than at each other. She typed *Curtain* and let it sit there, just that one word, and felt something in her chest loosen.

She didn't send those names. Not at first. She kept a second column in the spreadsheet, the true names, and then a first column, the ones Philip would get. *Hospital Curtain* became *Celadon Whisper*. *The Blue of the Pool at Your Sister's Wedding When We Were Still Pretending* became *Poolside*. She was, she realized, translating. She had always been translating. She just hadn't known what from.

---

Here's a thing people don't know about paint colors: the names matter enormously. Customers will not buy a color called *Mud*, but they will buy the identical pigment called *Riverbank*, and they'll feel good about it. They'll put it on their bedroom walls. They'll wake up inside it.

Marguerite used to find this cynical. Now she thinks it might be the most human thing she knows. We don't want the color. We want the story the color lets us tell about ourselves. Nobody lives in a gray box. They live in *Coastal Morning*, and it is always about to be a good day.

---

In March, David came by to pick up the last of his books. She'd boxed them herself, which felt either generous or hostile, and she still wasn't sure which. He stood in the living room and looked at the walls.

"You painted," he said.

She had. Two weekends, alone, windows open, cursing. The walls had been white when he lived there, a builder's white so flat it seemed to absorb sound. Now they were a pale, warm yellow, not quite butter, not quite straw. It was a color from the catalog. She'd named it herself, three years ago, back when the job was only a job.

"What's it called?" he asked.

He used to do this. When she first started, he'd read the catalog aloud in bed in a mock-seductive voice, *Mmm, Sandy Linen*, until she laughed so hard she cried. She had forgotten that. She had forgotten a great deal, on purpose, and here it was anyway, walking back in.

"*First Light*," she said.

He nodded slowly. He looked at the wall for a long moment and she could see him deciding whether to say something, the small tightening at the corner of his jaw that meant a sentence was being drafted and revised. Then he picked up the box.

"It's good," he said. "It suits the place."

After he left, she stood in the living room and looked at the wall herself. She thought about what she had actually been thinking, three years ago, when she named that yellow. It came back all at once: a Sunday, early, David asleep, the sun just reaching the bed and lighting up the side of his face, and her thinking with a kind of terror, *I am going to lose this someday. Everyone loses this.* She had named the color for that moment, the good version, the version without the terror. *First Light.* She'd sent it to Philip and he'd written back, *Perfect.*

---

Friday, she opened the new batch. Forty squares. She went through them slowly, and for each one she wrote the true name first, the one only she would see, and then the other one, the one that would go out into the world and onto people's walls.

The last square was a deep, clean blue, the blue of a sky about an hour after sunset, when the streetlights have come on but the day hasn't fully given up. She looked at it for a long time.

In the true column she wrote: *After.*

In the other column, after some thought, she wrote the same thing.

She sent it to Philip. He wrote back within the hour.

*Unusual,* he said. *But I think people will want to live there.*

Actually, I like another idea better—a story about someone who names paint colors, tying each name to a moment in her crumbling marriage. It feels specific and textured, so I'll go with that, titled "Eggshell, Linen, Bone," aiming for around 900 words.
